newsitem.title: USA: Clarke says he won't sell out economy to win election.
newsitem.headline: Clarke says he won't sell out economy to win election.

text.p: Britain's Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke, whose party faces an election in a few months lagging far behind in opinion polls, said on Sunday it would be foolish to tinker with the economy in the hope of picking up votes.

And he warned that any attempt to disrupt next week's Conservative party conference by right-wingers opposed to further integration with Europe would play into the hands of the opposition Labour Party.

"A government which intends to win an election does not make problems for itself by behaving foolishly a few months before," Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke told reporters during the annual IMF/World Bank meeting.
After 17 years in power, the Conservatives are behind in opinion polls, which point to a win by the Labour Party in the next general election that must be held by May.
"Electoral success depends on sensible, competent management of the national economy," Clarke said, warning that the last time his party had promised cuts it failed to deliver because of recession.

"The public would need to see that the tax cuts that can be made -- whenever they are made -- are credible, that they can be afforded, they are good for the national economy and that they are going to last," Clarke said.
Clarke insisted that any decision on interest rates also followed the dictates of economic common sense.
The Bank of England has said it would prefer to see rates slightly higher than the current 5.75 percent.
"If inflationary pressures begin to emerge and if it looks as though the inflation target will be at risk, then I would raise interest rates," he said.
"On the other hand...if there is an absence of inflationary pressure, it is obvious monetary policy is tight, then I'll relax interest rates. Otherwise I'll leave them alone," he added.
Apart from demand to loosen up on the economy, Clarke has also come under strong attack from within his party from right-wingers who see him as too willing to concede sovereignty to Brussels.

"I am sure they are planning no such thing," he said when asked how he would react if the so-called Eurosceptics would try to disrupt the Conservative party conference over their opposition to European Monetary Union.
"Such assistance to (Labour leader) Mr (Tony) Blair would be most unwelcome," he said.
Clarke said in a television interview that he expected the single European currency to go ahead, even though the January, 1999 deadline might slip.

"I think it is likely the Euro-zone is going to emerge. It is set upon by most of the Continental countries who intend to go into economic and monetary union. I think six, seven, eight of them will around the turn of the century," he said.
He insisted that he was fully behind Prime Minister John Major's position of keeping Britain's options open on whether to join a single currency.
